VBO:0200004.summary: The Afghan Hound often carries itself with dignified, somewhat aloof reserve, yet its urge to chase can be keen. Bred to pursue game by sight through Afghanistan’s mountains, it learned to make quick decisions while working at a distance from people. Early imports later captivated British dog shows; one named Zardin drew attention at London’s Crystal Palace in 1907.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 228: Afghan Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents Afghan mountain hunting and chase instinct, dignified/aloof temperament, and Zardin’s 1907 Crystal Palace appearance.

VBO:0200008.summary: The Airedale tends to be outgoing and confident, alert to its surroundings and friendly despite its terrier courage. It grew from Yorkshire’s waterside terriers into a notably versatile worker: it tracked by scent and later served police, military units and the Red Cross.
VBO:0200008.historicalRoots: Yorkshire waterside terrier developed for versatile work.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 7: Airedale Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard records Yorkshire waterside origin, tracking and wartime/police roles, plus outgoing, confident, friendly and courageous temperament.

VBO:0200016.summary: The Alaskan Klee Kai tends to be curious, quick and strongly attached to its people, though some are reserved with strangers and ready to sound an alarm. Linda Spurlin’s family developed it in Alaska as a small northern companion, retaining the watchful nature of spitz dogs. Its readiness to notice a change nearby is part of that active companion role.
VBO:0200016.historicalRoots: Alaskan companion breed developed from northern spitz-type dogs in the 1970s and 1980s.

sources.title: UKC Alaskan Klee Kai breed standard
sources.evidence: UKC standard documents Spurlin’s Alaskan development, toy/miniature/standard varieties, curiosity, agility, family attachment, stranger reserve and watchdog alarm.

VBO:0200034.summary: The American Bulldog tends to be steady and confident, with strong attachment to familiar people. Southern farmers preserved it as an all-purpose dog able to catch livestock and guard property; modern lines still reflect different emphases on stock work and guarding. The breed’s history includes a postwar rescue from near extinction.
VBO:0200034.interestingFact: John D. Johnson and Alan Scott led the postwar rebuilding effort.
VBO:0200034.historicalRoots: Southern U.S. farm and stock-working bulldog.

sources.title: UKC American Bulldog breed standard
sources.evidence: UKC standard details Southern farm catching and guarding, Johnson/Scott recovery, working-line differences, steady guardian disposition and family role.

VBO:0200047.summary: The American Foxhound is often easygoing in familiar company yet eager to follow a scent, with the endurance to stay on a fox trail beside other hounds. Colonial American hunters refined it for sustained pack work, where persistence mattered more than a quick burst. George Washington was among its early admirers.
VBO:0200047.historicalRoots: American pack hound developed for fox hunting.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 303: American Foxhound
sources.evidence: FCI identifies the American Foxhound as a scent hound developed for fox pursuit, with stamina for long pack hunts.

sources.title: AKC: What Hound Group Dogs Were Bred to Do
sources.evidence: AKC describes an easygoing temperament, endurance and work ethic in fox hunting, and George Washington’s admiration for the breed.

VBO:0200059.summary: The American Water Spaniel tends to bring enthusiasm to a hunt while staying friendly, responsive and cooperative with its handler. It was developed to retrieve from skiffs and canoes, then continue hunting on land—a practical partner for waterways too narrow for bigger boats.
VBO:0200059.historicalRoots: U.S. waterfowl and upland hunting dog.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 301: American Water Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI standard states skiff/canoe retrieval and land hunting, and describes friendly, eager-to-please temperament with energy and field control.

VBO:0200077.summary: The Armenian Gampr tends to watch for threats and decide when to respond, using the independent judgment its guardian work requires. It is a livestock guardian landrace shaped by the Armenian Highlands, where protecting flocks and family holdings mattered more than uniform looks. Regional working populations retain meaningful variation.
VBO:0200077.historicalRoots: Armenian Highlands livestock and homestead guardian.

sources.title: Armenian Gampr Club breed description
sources.evidence: Armenian Gampr Club identifies Armenian Highland guardian work, landrace variation and independent protective judgment.

VBO:0200097.summary: The Australian Stumpy Tail Cattle Dog tends to be loyal, courageous and watchful, sometimes suspicious of strangers. It was selected for moving cattle across hard Australian country, with a natural aptitude for controlling stock. The droving role asked it to keep stock moving for long distances while staying attentive to both cattle and country.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 351: Australian Stumpy Tail Cattle Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents cattle-droving origin, innate stock-working aptitude, loyal/watchful disposition and differing early ancestry accounts.

VBO:0200103.summary: The Austrian Pinscher is typically lively and playful with familiar people, yet alert and suspicious enough to watch the homestead. It descends from the versatile country dogs once common around Austrian farms. Its hunting drive tends to be mild, while the alertness and readiness to bark fit the old farm-watch job.
VBO:0200103.historicalRoots: Austrian farm dog refined through twentieth-century breeding.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 64: Austrian Pinscher
sources.evidence: FCI standard traces Austrian farm use and breeding milestones, and describes lively, familiar-friendly, stranger-suspicious watchdog temperament with slight hunting instinct.

VBO:0200121.summary: The Basque Shepherd Dog’s Iletsua variety tends to work closely with its person and strongly mark its territory. It comes from the pastoral life of Spain’s Basque country, where close partnership and sustained attention to livestock mattered in daily herding. The breed also includes a second documented variety, Gorbeiakoa.
VBO:0200121.historicalRoots: Basque livestock herding dog with Iletsua and Gorbeiakoa varieties.

sources.title: RSCE Basque Shepherd Dog, Iletsua standard
sources.evidence: RSCE Iletsua standard identifies Basque herding work, close owner bond and territorial behavior.

sources.title: RSCE Basque Shepherd Dog, Gorbeiakoa standard
sources.evidence: RSCE documents Gorbeiakoa as another Basque Shepherd Dog variety.

VBO:0200126.summary: The Basset Hound is often placid and affectionate away from a scent trail, though its pack instinct and deep voice come alive during a hunt. It was made to follow hare scent through heavy cover at a pace people could keep up with. This blend of patient pursuit, sociability with other hounds and easygoing company follows from its slow, determined style of hunting.
VBO:0200126.historicalRoots: French basset hunting roots; developed further in Britain for hare trailing.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 163: Basset Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard covers hare trailing through cover over distance, scent hunting, pack instinct, deep voice and placid affectionate temperament.

VBO:0200136.summary: The Beauceron tends to be self-assured, gentle and fearless, alert enough to take responsibility without a frantic manner. It was selected on French plains to conduct and guard sheep flocks, work that called for both confidence and composure. Moving and guarding a flock were linked jobs, so it needed to follow a shepherd’s direction while keeping watch for trouble.
VBO:0200136.historicalRoots: French plains sheepdog selected for flock driving and guarding.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 44: Beauceron
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents French plains flock-driving and guarding, confident gentle fearless temperament and Bas Rouge nickname.

VBO:0200158.summary: The Berger Picard tends to be an even-tempered, obedient and fearless worker that also values close contact with its household. Its sheep-and-cattle herding roots show in its job of moving and protecting a flock. After World War II, fanciers searched Picardy for typical dogs to revive interest in this old regional type.
VBO:0200158.historicalRoots: French rough-coated sheep and cattle herder, revived after World War II.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 176: Berger Picard
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents flock driving/protection, even temperament and household contact, plus postwar Picardy revival work.

VBO:0200168.summary: The Black and Tan Coonhound tends to be outgoing and friendly while working closely with other hounds. On a hunt it follows a raccoon entirely by scent, then signals when the animal is treed. Persistence through difficult ground in heat or cold is part of the job, and the breed has also followed larger game.
VBO:0200168.historicalRoots: American scent hound developed for raccoon trailing and treeing.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 300: Black and Tan Coonhound
sources.evidence: FCI details scent-only raccoon trailing and treeing, pack compatibility, friendly outgoing temperament, all-season terrain work and use on larger game.

VBO:0200186.summary: The Bohemian Shepherd tends to be lively but controlled: attentive, vigilant and trainable, with a strong sense of smell. It belongs to a Czech tradition of guarding holdings and rounding up cattle. Stories of guarding and cattle-driving dogs have been part of the Chodsko region for centuries.
VBO:0200186.historicalRoots: Czech herding and homestead-guarding tradition associated with Chodsko.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 364: Bohemian Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard records Chodsko guarding/cattle history with pedigree caution, and describes vigilance, scenting ability and responsive trainability.

VBO:0200194.summary: The Border Terrier is active and game, eager to stay with a hunt even when it moves from open ground into a narrow earth. On the England–Scotland border it had to keep pace with horses above ground, then pursue quarry where larger hunting partners could not follow. That two-part work called for stamina, agility and determined terrier courage.
VBO:0200194.historicalRoots: Border-country working terrier for mounted hunts and earth work.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 10: Border Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI describes the Border Terrier as active and game, able to keep up with horses and enter an earth after quarry.

sources.title: AKC: Border Terrier facts
sources.evidence: AKC locates the breed along the England–Scotland border and explains the combined above-ground and underground work.

VBO:0200208.summary: The Bouvier des Flandres tends to be calm, thoughtful and fearless, qualities that mattered when handling large stock. Flanders cattle drovers selected the Bouvier des Flandres to move herds across farms on both sides of today’s Belgian–French border. Drovers relied on a dog able to keep moving among animals while listening and adjusting to its handler.
VBO:0200208.historicalRoots: Flanders cattle drover from Belgian and French farming communities.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 191: Bouvier des Flandres
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents Flanders cattle-driving origin and the calm, thoughtful, fearless temperament expected of a working Bouvier.

VBO:0200215.summary: The Bracco Italiano tends to be tough across varied hunting terrain yet notably docile and responsive to training. It has centuries of Italian bird-hunting history, with a broad, fast trot valued for covering ground and pointing game. It is also an able retriever.
VBO:0200215.historicalRoots: Italian bird-hunting pointer with longstanding field tradition.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 202: Bracco Italiano
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents old Italian bird-hunting roots, pointing and retrieving, wide trot, varied hunting ability and docile trainability.

VBO:0200238.summary: The Brittany tends to be sociable and attentive, with a keen nose, spontaneous point and reliable retrieve in the field. It was developed in France as a versatile pointing dog for game on varied terrain. Its field work asks it to search independently, then cooperate closely with the hunter when it finds game.
VBO:0200238.historicalRoots: French Brittany pointing dog; formal standard adopted in 1908.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 95: Brittany
sources.evidence: FCI standard details Brittany origin, all-terrain pointing, scenting, retrieving, sociability and early short-tail club name.

VBO:0200261.summary: The Bullmastiff tends to be enduring, alert and faithful; reliable judgment was as important as force in its difficult night-watch role. Its early job was helping British gamekeepers stop poachers, using strength and nerve to apprehend rather than chase over long distances. Mastiff and bulldog ancestry supplied the foundation for that guarding role.
VBO:0200261.historicalRoots: British gamekeeper’s guard dog developed from mastiff and bulldog stock.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 157: Bullmastiff
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents gamekeeper/poacher work, Mastiff–Bulldog ancestry and enduring, alert, faithful temperament.

VBO:0200271.summary: The Campeiro Bulldog tends to be vigilant yet calm and responsive to its handler even during demanding cattle work. It arose in southern Brazil as a cattle-catching dog, helping locate, hold and move difficult stock through fields and native scrub. The same dogs also served at old slaughterhouses, another part of the breed’s rural past.
VBO:0200271.historicalRoots: Southern Brazilian cattle-catching and farm-guarding bulldog.

sources.title: CBKC Brazilian Campeiro Bulldog standard
sources.evidence: CBKC standard documents southern Brazilian cattle work, old slaughterhouse use and vigilant, calm, handler-responsive temperament.

VBO:0200290.summary: The Cardigan Welsh Corgi tends to be alert, active and intelligent with a steady manner. It grew from a cattle-driving tradition that demanded mobility and endurance around large animals. Its farm work linked close attention to livestock with daily partnership at home.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 38: Cardigan Welsh Corgi
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies herding and companion uses, endurance and mobility, and alert, active, intelligent, steady temperament.

VBO:0200309.summary: The Cavalier King Charles Spaniel tends to meet people with an affectionate, friendly manner while retaining a game, active streak. It carries two traditions at once: British lap companion and small sporting spaniel. Its modern line was revived in the twentieth century to recall the spaniels seen around Charles II’s court.
VBO:0200309.interestingFact: The Duke of Marlborough’s Blenheim spaniels were valued for both lap warming and bird hunting.
VBO:0200309.historicalRoots: British toy spaniel developed as a companion.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 136: Cavalier King Charles Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI describes the Cavalier as sporting, affectionate and friendly, with an active temperament.

sources.title: AKC: Cavalier King Charles Spaniel History
sources.evidence: AKC documents the Charles II royal association, twentieth-century revival, and old Blenheim dogs used for both lap companionship and bird hunting.

VBO:0200326.summary: The Chesapeake Bay Retriever tends to show courage, a keen nose and a love of water alongside quiet good sense and an affectionate, protective nature. It was developed for waterfowl work in rough weather, often facing cold swims, strong tides and repeated retrieves. The demanding bay work helps explain both its persistence and its practical judgment.
VBO:0200326.interestingFact: Its waterfowl work could require breaking ice to reach a bird.
VBO:0200326.historicalRoots: Chesapeake Bay waterfowl retriever bred for severe conditions.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 263: Chesapeake Bay Retriever
sources.evidence: FCI standard details Chesapeake waterfowl work in tides, ice and cold, and lists courage, scenting, water affinity, good sense and protective affection.

VBO:0200353.summary: The Chinook tends to be a calm, willing worker that cooperates with other dogs, though some are reserved with strangers. It was built for teamwork on sleds, combining freight-hauling strength with the pace of racing dogs. The line traces to Arthur Walden’s single 1917 foundation dog, who later joined Byrd’s Antarctic expedition.
VBO:0200353.historicalRoots: New Hampshire sled dog developed in the early twentieth century.

sources.title: UKC Chinook breed standard
sources.evidence: UKC standard documents team sled work, freight/racing aims, calm cooperative disposition, stranger reserve, 1917 foundation dog and Antarctic expedition.

VBO:0200364.summary: The Cimarrón Uruguayo tends to be balanced, intelligent and courageous, traits later valued for guarding estates and working cattle. Its ancestors descended from dogs introduced to Uruguay during the colonial era, then survived as free-ranging animals. The exact early mix is uncertain, but the move from survival to purposeful stock work is central to its story.
VBO:0200364.historicalRoots: Uruguayan cattle and estate guardian descended from introduced colonial dogs.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 353: Cimarron Uruguayo
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes colonial descent with uncertain origin, free-ranging selection, later estate guarding and cattle work, and balanced courageous temperament.

VBO:0200392.summary: The Croatian Sheepdog tends to be devoted, lively and level-headed, staying interested in its surroundings without becoming nervous. It has long worked livestock in eastern Slavonia, using quick reactions and sustained attention around moving animals. Its quick responses help it turn and redirect livestock as the flock moves.
VBO:0200392.historicalRoots: Eastern Slavonian livestock herder; systematic breeding from 1935.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 277: Croatian Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies eastern Slavonian livestock work, inherited herding sense, lively devoted level-headed behavior and 1930s breeding.

VBO:0200427.summary: The Dalmatian has a lively, independent streak, a marked hunting instinct and an affinity for water and outdoor activity. Its association with carriages grew alongside these active tendencies. Spotted dogs appear in Croatian regional art and church records from the seventeenth century, tying the breed’s name and history to Dalmatia.
VBO:0200427.historicalRoots: Croatian Dalmatian-region hound with later coach-dog history.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 153: Dalmatian
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents Dalmatian regional art and coach-dog history, plus independent, lively temperament, hound instinct and water/outdoor interest.

VBO:0200442.summary: The Doberman tends to be calm and devoted in familiar company while staying attentive to its surroundings. Friedrich Louis Dobermann developed his namesake dog in nineteenth-century Germany for protective work, and the breed later served police forces. Confidence, willingness to work and responsiveness to training helped carry it into demanding service roles.
VBO:0200442.interestingFact: Early police service gave the Doberman the nickname “Gendarme dog.”
VBO:0200442.historicalRoots: German protective working dog developed by Friedrich Louis Dobermann.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 143: Doberman Pinscher
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents Friedrich Louis Dobermann, protection and police use, and calm, family-devoted, attentive, trainable working temperament.

VBO:0200450.summary: The Dogue de Bordeaux tends to be watchful and courageous, often calm and deeply attached to familiar people. It has a long Aquitaine history that includes guarding homes and cattle and, earlier, hunting large game. It nearly disappeared after the world wars before a postwar revival.
VBO:0200450.historicalRoots: French molosser of Aquitaine, historically a guard and big-game dog.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 116: Dogue de Bordeaux
sources.evidence: FCI standard records Aquitaine origins, guarding and big-game roles, postwar recovery, and vigilant, courageous, calm, affectionate temperament.

VBO:0200456.summary: The Dunker tends to be sociable and trusting as well as robust on a hunt, with a steady manner that has served in field trials. Wilhelm Conrad Dunker developed his Norwegian scent hound for hare hunting, bringing together local working lines in the nineteenth century. Later controlled outcrossing helped maintain genetic variety in a small population.
VBO:0200456.historicalRoots: Norwegian hare hound developed by Wilhelm Conrad Dunker.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 203: Dunker
sources.evidence: FCI standard names creator and hare work, describes sociable, trusting and trainable temperament, and recounts trials and outcrossing for diversity.

VBO:0200490.summary: The English Foxhound tends to be friendly and sociable, with the stamina and natural hunting drive to keep pace in a pack. It was developed for long collective work on fox scent during mounted hunts. English hunt masters kept pedigrees for generations, leaving studbooks that reach back before 1800.
VBO:0200490.historicalRoots: English pack hound with documented fox-hunting lines.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 159: English Foxhound
sources.evidence: FCI describes the English Foxhound as friendly, nonaggressive, enduring and naturally inclined to hunt; it records long-running hunt-master studbooks.

sources.title: UKC: English Foxhound Breed Standard
sources.evidence: UKC says the English Foxhound was bred to trail red foxes during mounted hunts and describes its friendly, enduring pack-hunting character.

VBO:0200502.summary: The Entlebuch Cattle Dog tends to be lively and confident, devoted to familiar faces yet somewhat suspicious of strangers. It comes from a Swiss valley where it drove stock, watched farms and worked close to people. Both driving cattle and watching the farm rewarded a dog that noticed changes quickly and stayed close to its people.
VBO:0200502.historicalRoots: Swiss Entlebuch valley stock driver and farm guard.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 47: Entlebuch Cattle Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Entlebuch stock-driving and watch roles, smallest Swiss mountain-dog status, lively confidence and familiar devotion with stranger caution.

VBO:0200512.summary: The Eurasier tends to be calm and closely attached to family, attentive without constant noise and more reserved than pushy with strangers. German breeders developed it specifically for companionship, beginning with Chow Chow and Wolfspitz crosses and later adding Samoyed. Quiet watchfulness remains part of that companion role.
VBO:0200512.interestingFact: It was first called the Wolf-Chow before the Samoyed cross led to the Eurasier name.
VBO:0200512.historicalRoots: German companion spitz founded by Julius Wipfel in the 1960s.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 291: Eurasier
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents founding crosses and companion purpose, plus calm, family-bonded, watchful, non-noisy and stranger-reserved temperament.

VBO:0200523.summary: The Finnish Lapphund tends to combine courage and calm with a friendly, responsive manner, a useful balance around shifting livestock and people. It grew from dogs Sámi communities used to herd reindeer across northern Fennoscandia. In Finland it has also become a familiar companion, while that northern working history remains central.
VBO:0200523.historicalRoots: Sámi reindeer-herding tradition in northern Fennoscandia.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 189: Finnish Lapphund
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts Sámi reindeer work and later companionship, and describes courageous, calm, docile, friendly temperament.

VBO:0201455.summary: The French Bulldog tends to be lively, playful and sociable, eager to stay involved with its people. It took shape among Parisian porters, butchers and coachmen before finding favor in the city’s artistic and social circles. The Paris street-to-salon path is part of its distinct story.
VBO:0201455.historicalRoots: Parisian companion dog developed in the late nineteenth century.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 101: French Bulldog
sources.evidence: FCI standard dates Parisian working-class ownership and later popularity, and characterizes the breed as sociable, lively, playful and keen on companionship.

VBO:0200563.summary: The Georgian Shepherd tends to be watchful and capable of independent action, enduring harsh conditions as it guards. Also called the Kartuli Nagazi, it developed in Georgia’s mountains as a protective dog for people and holdings. Its work called for noticing danger, making decisions and staying on duty across scattered mountain communities.
VBO:0200563.historicalRoots: Georgian mountain guardian and pastoral dog.

sources.title: Elkana Georgian agricultural biodiversity: Georgian Shepherd
sources.evidence: Elkana Georgian agricultural biodiversity account locates the type in Georgian mountains and describes protective instinct, vigilance, independent behavior and tolerance of difficult conditions.

VBO:0200583.summary: The German Shorthaired Pointer tends to be firm, balanced and reliable, with a working temperament that is neither nervous nor easily unsettled. Bred as an all-purpose gundog, it can point game, follow a trail and retrieve after the shot. German breeders used field trials to keep that versatile working ability central.
VBO:0200583.historicalRoots: German all-purpose pointing dog refined from European bird-hunting lines.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 119: German Shorthaired Pointer
sources.evidence: FCI standard traces German all-purpose gundog development, pointing/retrieving/tracking function, trials and firm balanced temperament.

VBO:0200609.summary: The Glen of Imaal Terrier often combines courage when needed with a relatively quiet, less easily excited manner than some terriers. It comes from an Irish valley where dogs had to hunt foxes and badgers and help control rats. Older accounts even describe Glen dogs turning wheels in farm households.
VBO:0200609.historicalRoots: Irish Glen of Imaal farm terrier selected for hard local work.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 302: Glen of Imaal Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents Irish farm hunting and ratting, quiet working manner, lower excitability and historical dog-wheel use.

VBO:0200629.summary: The Great Pyrenees tends to act independently while staying attached to the animals it protects, often deterring danger before it closes in. It was selected to guard mountain flocks against predators, often making judgments without constant direction. The breed later entered French court life, but its core story remains the long pastoral watch.
VBO:0200629.interestingFact: The Pyrenean guardian was known at Louis XIV’s court after centuries of mountain use.
VBO:0200629.historicalRoots: Pyrenean flock guardian with medieval castle associations.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 137: Great Pyrenees
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents flock guarding, predator deterrence, independent initiative, attachment to flock and later French-court association.

VBO:0200638.summary: The Greyhound often shows a gentle, even-tempered and affectionate disposition away from the chase, yet has stamina for sustained pursuit. Its old work was sighting and coursing hare, with racing emerging from that pursuit tradition. Coursing asks for quick decisions at speed as well as the ability to stay focused on moving game.
VBO:0200638.historicalRoots: British-developed hare-coursing sighthound later used in racing.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 158: Greyhound
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts hare coursing and racing development, and describes stamina, gentle affection and even temperament.

VBO:0200667.summary: The Hellenic Hound keeps following scent across difficult ground and uses a strong, musical voice to signal progress. It works from Greek lowlands to rocky mountain trails, sometimes alone and sometimes with a pack. That combination of persistence, vocal trail work and adaptable hunting ground defines its less visible character.
VBO:0200667.historicalRoots: Greek scent hound traditionally worked over varied, rocky terrain.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 214: Hellenic Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Greek origin, solo or pack scent hunting across lowland/mountain/rocky terrain, resistance and resonant voice.

VBO:0200678.summary: The Magyar Agár tends to be watchful and sensible, sometimes reserved but not shy, with a protective instinct toward home and people. It is a Hungarian hunting sighthound with stamina for sustained pursuit, not only short-distance speed. Nineteenth-century breeders crossed other sighthounds into the old type to increase pace.
VBO:0200678.historicalRoots: Hungarian hunting sighthound with medieval roots and nineteenth-century refinement.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 240: Hungarian Greyhound
sources.evidence: FCI standard records Hungarian hunting history, later speed crosses, racing stamina, reserve, sense and watchful protective tendency.

VBO:0200692.summary: The Icelandic Sheepdog tends to be cheerful, curious and confident, traits shaped by daily partnership on island farms. It helped farmers round up livestock in Iceland’s difficult terrain after dogs arrived with Viking settlers. It uses barking in herding and also tends to announce visitors, often greeting people with friendly interest.
VBO:0200692.interestingFact: The first settlers brought ancestral dogs to Iceland around AD 870–930.
VBO:0200692.historicalRoots: Icelandic farm and livestock dog descending from settler dogs.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 289: Icelandic Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents settler history and livestock work, barking in herding and visitor alerts, and cheerful inquisitive confident temperament.

VBO:0200702.summary: The Irish Setter tends to be keen and energetic in the field while affectionate and loyal in familiar company. It began as a red bird dog selected for searching and setting game with stamina in the field. The Irish Red Setter Club has paired field trials with shows since the nineteenth century, keeping both sides of the breed visible.
VBO:0200702.historicalRoots: Irish red setter developed for bird hunting.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 120: Irish Setter
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Irish bird-hunting work, energetic affectionate loyalty and longstanding field-trial tradition.

VBO:0200709.summary: The Istrian Short-Haired Hound tends to be persistent and trainable on a hunt, gentle with familiar people and wary of strangers. It is prized in Croatia for following game through stony Karst country, where its strong, melodic voice carries across rough ground. Regional art records similar hounds centuries before modern breeding.
VBO:0200709.historicalRoots: Croatian Adriatic hare and fox scent hound.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 151: Istrian Short-Haired Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Karst hunting, melodic voice, training response, gentle owner devotion, stranger wariness and old Adriatic depictions.

VBO:0200721.summary: The Italian Spinone pairs toughness in the field with a patient, sociable and docile manner. It works across difficult hunting ground: it can push through thorny cover, enter cold water and retrieve game. Old Italian paintings and hunting writing point to rough-haired dogs of this type long before modern field trials.
VBO:0200721.historicalRoots: Italian rough-haired pointing dog with longstanding field use.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 165: Italian Spinone
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents thorny-cover and cold-water work, retrieval, patience and sociability, plus early Italian art references.

VBO:0200733.summary: The Jämthund tends to be energetic and courageous when elk hunting yet capable of stoic calm. It is a Swedish elk hunter expected to find and bay game for long stretches, a task that needs endurance and nerve. The breed was long grouped with the smaller Norwegian Elkhound before gaining separate recognition in 1946.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 42: Jämthund
sources.evidence: FCI standard details elk-baying use, endurance, courageous/energetic yet stoically calm temperament and 1946 separate recognition.

VBO:0200741.summary: The Japanese Terrier tends to be lively and swift, with an animated temperament suited to quick play and close companionship. It began in Japan’s port cities, where imported fox terriers mixed with small local dogs. Families in Kobe and Yokohama kept it chiefly as a companion, though its fast terrier response remained part of its character.
VBO:0200741.historicalRoots: Japanese port-city companion terrier refined in the early twentieth century.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 259: Japanese Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts imported-terrier ancestry, Kobe/Yokohama lapdog role, early planned breeding and swift lively temperament.

VBO:0200751.summary: The Kanni is known in southern Tamil Nadu for fast pursuit on a hunt and for companionship with local families. Its traditional work calls for agility and sustained attention to moving game. The documented breeding tract centers on Virudhunagar, Tuticorin and Tirunelveli, where these roles remain part of its regional identity.
VBO:0200751.historicalRoots: Tamil Nadu indigenous hound associated with hunting and companionship.

sources.title: Selvakkumar et al., Morphometric Characterization of Kanni Dog
sources.evidence: Original Indian Veterinary Journal field study identifies Kanni hunting and companion roles, agility and fast-hunting structure, and southern Tamil Nadu breeding tract.

VBO:0200759.summary: The Keeshond tends to be outgoing and friendly while staying ready to bark when someone approaches its home. It served on Dutch canal barges as both a watch dog and a close companion, alert to arrivals without losing its sociable side. Its association with the Dutch Patriot movement made it a political symbol as well as a household one.
VBO:0200759.interestingFact: The breed name is linked to Kees, a Dutch Patriot leader whose party adopted the dog as a mascot.
VBO:0200759.historicalRoots: Dutch barge companion and watchdog with spitz ancestry.

sources.title: UKC Keeshond breed standard
sources.evidence: UKC standard documents barge guarding/companionship, outgoing friendliness, other historic uses and Patriot movement association.

VBO:0200774.summary: The Kishu Ken tends to be alert, enduring, faithful and responsive, traits useful when tracking and confronting wild boar. It was shaped in Japan’s Kishu mountains for hunting, now especially wild boar. The breed’s regional identity was formally honored in Japan as a natural monument in 1934.
VBO:0200774.historicalRoots: Kishu mountain hunter used mainly for wild boar.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 318: Kishu Ken
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Kishu mountain origin, boar/deer hunting, endurance, faithful alert temperament and 1934 natural-monument designation.

VBO:0200786.summary: The Kromfohrländer tends to be spirited, adaptable and docile, sometimes reserved with strangers and usually showing only a modest hunting instinct. It was developed near Siegen, Germany, as a companion rather than a specialist hunter. The breed’s unusual name comes from the local Krom Fohr district, home to its first breeder.
VBO:0200786.historicalRoots: German companion breed developed near Siegen in the mid-twentieth century.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 192: Kromfohrlander
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes companion purpose, adaptable docile high-spirited temperament, mild hunting instinct, stranger reserve and Krom Fohr name origin.

VBO:0200814.summary: The Lapponian Herder may bark readily while working yet often remains calm, friendly and willing in other settings. Sámi herders used dogs of this tradition to move reindeer, a job that rewards a steady pace and close attention to the herd. Finnish breeders later distinguished it from the Finnish Lapphund as a separate reindeer-working type.
VBO:0200814.historicalRoots: Sámi reindeer-herding dog of northern Finland.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 284: Lapponian Herder
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents Sámi reindeer work, work-time barking, calm willing temperament and 1966 breed separation.

VBO:0200824.summary: The Lhasa Apso tends to be alert and self-possessed, sometimes keeping a little distance from strangers while remaining steady with its own circle. It was shaped by Tibet’s high-altitude climate and later reached Britain in the 1920s. Early British fanciers confused it with other shaggy Tibetan dogs before recognizing the Apso separately.
VBO:0200824.historicalRoots: Tibetan highland companion; introduced to Britain in the 1920s.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 227: Lhasa Apso
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts Tibetan origin and British arrival, alert assertive stranger-aloof temperament and early confusion with related Tibetan dogs.

VBO:0200862.summary: The Manchester Terrier tends to be keen and alert, yet discerning and devoted in close company. It earned its name in an English city where ratting contests and pub shows helped make it a recognizable breed. The city’s ratting culture gave this keen little terrier a practical nineteenth-century job.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 71: Manchester Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents Manchester ratting and pub-show history, plus keen alert sporting and devoted temperament.

VBO:0200893.summary: The Miniature Pinscher is a German companion pinscher with a lively, self-assured temperament. It tends to be quick to notice its surroundings, spirited in activity and even in familiar company. German pinscher lines gave it a history of its own as a close household dog.
VBO:0200893.historicalRoots: German small pinscher established before the twentieth century.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 185: Miniature Pinscher
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies German companion use, lively spirited self-assured even temperament and the 1925 studbook total.

VBO:0200920.summary: The Mudhol Hound is valued for speed and stamina in open-country pursuit across northern Karnataka and the western Deccan. Regional families have used it for hunting, guarding and companionship, linking a keen chase response with watch duties near home. Its working history is especially associated with villages around Bagalkot.
VBO:0200920.historicalRoots: Karnataka sighthound of the western Deccan.

sources.title: Dodamani et al., Physical and Performance Characteristics of Mudhol Hound Dogs
sources.evidence: Karnataka university field study identifies northern Karnataka tract, hunting/guarding/companion roles, speed and stamina, and a 150-dog survey.

VBO:0200932.summary: The Nederlandse Kooikerhondje tends to be alert and energetic, persistent at work without being needlessly noisy. At a Dutch duck decoy it moves between reed screens and waves its tail to draw curious ducks into a trap; it does not retrieve them. It also historically hunted vermin, giving this small working spaniel two distinctive jobs.
VBO:0200932.historicalRoots: Dutch duck-decoy worker revived in the 1940s.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 314: Nederlandse Kooikerhondje
sources.evidence: FCI standard details duck-decoy luring rather than retrieval, off-season vermin work, alert energetic non-noisy temperament and Tommy’s wartime role.

VBO:0200953.summary: The Norwegian Buhund tends to be courageous and energetic but also friendly, a combination suited to daily work alongside people. It was a versatile farmstead dog, helping herd livestock and keeping watch around Norwegian holdings. The name itself points to the farmstead, and old accounts place buhund-type dogs in Norway far back toward the Viking Age.
VBO:0200953.historicalRoots: Norwegian farm, herding and watch dog with old spitz roots.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 237: Norwegian Buhund
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents Norwegian herding/watch use, courageous energetic friendly character, name meaning and Viking-era history.

VBO:0200964.summary: The Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever tends to be quick to fetch, intelligent and trainable, with the endurance to swim for game. It plays an unusual two-part hunting role: its playful movement near shore draws waterfowl closer, and then it retrieves them from land or water.
VBO:0200964.historicalRoots: Nova Scotian waterfowl tolling and retrieving dog of the nineteenth century.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 312: Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever
sources.evidence: FCI standard explains Nova Scotian tolling and retrieval, playful lure behavior, retrieving desire, intelligence, training response and swimming endurance.

VBO:0200980.summary: The Otterhound is often amiable and even-tempered away from the demanding scent work for which it was bred. It followed scent over both bank and water, announcing a promising trail with its deep bay. Houndsmen distinguished a land “drag” from a waterborne “wash,” and the breed was built to keep going through either.
VBO:0200980.historicalRoots: British otter-trailing scent hound, a former hunting role.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 294: Otterhound
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents otter tracking on land and water, drag/wash terms, bay, hunting ban and amiable even temperament.

VBO:0200995.summary: The Pembroke Welsh Corgi tends to be bold, outgoing and friendly, with stamina to keep moving as livestock changes direction. It was bred to work sheep and cattle, staying mobile and alert around animals much larger than itself. The farm role rewarded initiative as well as a close response to its handler.
VBO:0200995.historicalRoots: Welsh cattle herder with a compact low build.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 39: Pembroke Welsh Corgi
sources.evidence: FCI standard lists sheepdog/cattledog function and describes workmanlike boldness, friendliness and stamina.

VBO:0201032.summary: The Chart Polski tends to be self-assured, brave and sometimes reserved rather than immediately familiar. In pursuit it is fast, skillful and tireless, reacting quickly when game moves. This Polish hunting sighthound appears in records from the thirteenth century, giving its chase instinct a long regional history.
VBO:0201032.historicalRoots: Polish hunting sighthound documented since the medieval period.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 333: Polish Greyhound
sources.evidence: FCI describes medieval Polish hunting records, self-assured and brave but reserved temperament, quick reaction and fast untiring pursuit.

VBO:0201048.summary: The Poodle tends to be loyal and quick to learn, carrying cooperative traits from its waterfowl-hunting roots into work and play. It once entered water to retrieve birds, then became a notably trainable companion. The French name caniche still points back to ducks and the breed’s old retrieving role.
VBO:0201048.historicalRoots: French waterfowl dog of Barbet-related ancestry, later a companion in four sizes.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 172: Poodle
sources.evidence: FCI standard traces wildfowling and Barbet-related origins, loyalty and trainability, caniche etymology and four FCI size varieties.

VBO:0201071.summary: The Portuguese Sheepdog tends to be lively and deeply focused on its shepherd and herd, with a watchful streak that helped alert to predators. It worked the Alentejo plains, keeping sheep, cattle, goats, horses and pigs together and searching for strays. That range of livestock and the distances between pastures made versatility essential.
VBO:0201071.historicalRoots: Alentejo all-purpose livestock herder and watcher.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 93: Portuguese Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents five Alentejo livestock types, searching for strays, vigilance toward predators and lively shepherd-focused working temperament.

VBO:0201089.summary: The Pug tends to be lively, happy and even-tempered, with a sociable manner that suited close companionship. Its story runs from China to Europe through Dutch trade, where it became a symbol for royalist supporters in the Netherlands. That court association placed the breed at the center of a very different kind of public life.
VBO:0201089.historicalRoots: Chinese companion dog spread to Europe through Dutch trade.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 253: Pug
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes China-to-Europe route through Dutch traders, Dutch royal-patriot symbolism and happy lively even temperament.

VBO:0000670.summary: The Pyrenean Mastiff tends to be calm and friendly with familiar people, yet uses a deep warning bark when guarding. It once protected Spanish mountain flocks from wolves and bears, a role that required courage without constant agitation. Its watchfulness still reflects that old predator-defense work in the Pyrenees.
VBO:0000670.historicalRoots: Spanish Pyrenean livestock guardian against large predators.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 92: Pyrenean Mastiff
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies wolf/bear defense, guarding use, calm human-friendly disposition, courage toward threats and deep bark.

VBO:0201132.summary: The Redbone Coonhound tends to be even-tempered and affectionate, with a strong wish to please and a natural instinct to tree game. It follows raccoon scent over varied terrain and signals when quarry is treed; it can also work in water. Georgia breeder George F. L. Birdsong supplied important foundation stock to the line.
VBO:0201132.historicalRoots: U.S. raccoon-trailing and treeing hound with Georgia foundation lines.

sources.title: UKC Redbone Coonhound breed standard
sources.evidence: UKC describes even temper, affection, desire to please, treeing instinct and water ability; it also records raccoon trailing and George F. L. Birdsong’s foundation stock.

VBO:0201143.summary: The Rottweiler tends to be self-assured, steady and eager to work, staying alert without losing an even temper. Its working story runs through cattle driving, guarding and pulling loads in the German town of Rottweil. Butchers favored the breed for usefulness, and police service later drew on the same combination of nerve and willingness.
VBO:0201143.interestingFact: The old working name was “Rottweil butcher’s dog.”
VBO:0201143.historicalRoots: German cattle drover and guard dog associated with Rottweil.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 147: Rottweiler
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts Rottweil droving, guarding, draft and police work, butcher association and steady biddable alert temperament.

VBO:0201180.summary: The Šarplaninac tends to be reliable, protective and devoted to its handler, with an even disposition rather than a quick, indiscriminate reaction. It guarded cattle herds against predators in the mountain region that gave the breed its name. The role continues an old Balkan livestock-guardian tradition.
VBO:0201180.historicalRoots: Balkan livestock guardian of the Šar mountain region.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 41: Sarplaninac
sources.evidence: FCI standard locates the breed in the Šar mountain region, documents cattle-herd predator protection, and describes reliable, even and protective temperament.

VBO:0201185.summary: The Schnauzer is typically playful and devoted with familiar people, alert to intruders yet not expected to bark without pause. It began as a southern German stable dog, keeping company with horses and dispatching rodents around the yard. The early nickname “Rattler” captures the practical job beneath today’s companion role.
VBO:0201185.historicalRoots: Southern German stable and rodent-control dog.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 182: Schnauzer
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents southern German stable/ratter work, horse association, playful devotion and alert-but-not-noisy temperament.

VBO:0201200.summary: The Sealyham Terrier tends to be game and fearless on the job but friendly in ordinary company. It was developed in Wales for hard terrier work alongside otterhounds and against vermin. Captain John Edwardes shaped the strain at his Sealy Ham estate, giving the dog both its name and a very specific working origin.
VBO:0201200.historicalRoots: Welsh earth-working terrier later kept as a companion.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 74: Sealyham Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI describes the Sealyham as game, fearless and friendly.

sources.title: AKC: Sealyham Terrier history
sources.evidence: AKC traces Captain John Edwardes’s development of the Sealyham at his Welsh estate for vermin and otter work.

VBO:0201223.summary: The Shih Tzu tends to be friendly, alert and independent, carrying a self-possessed manner into close companionship. It has Tibetan roots but grew into a favored companion in Chinese imperial palaces before spreading west. British imports in the 1930s helped establish the modern Western population.
VBO:0201223.historicalRoots: Tibetan roots and Chinese palace development as a companion dog.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 208: Shih Tzu
sources.evidence: FCI standard distinguishes Tibetan roots and Chinese palace development, identifies friendly independent alert temperament and dates British introduction.

VBO:0201237.summary: The Silky Terrier tends to be active, keenly alert and courageous, ready to investigate movement with the quick response of a terrier. It emerged in Australia from local terrier and Yorkshire lines and became a close companion without losing that inquisitive spirit. Early breeders shaped the type around Sydney before it spread more widely.
VBO:0201237.historicalRoots: Australian companion terrier shaped from local and Yorkshire lines.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 236: Silky Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents Australian/Yorkshire ancestry and Sydney development, and describes keen alertness, activity, courage and companionship.

VBO:0201278.summary: The Spanish Mastiff tends to pair affection toward familiar people with resolve when stock or property is threatened. It traveled with Merino flocks on seasonal routes, staying close enough to defend animals from wolves in changing pastures. Its story is inseparable from Spain’s old transhumant sheep culture and the medieval Mesta.
VBO:0201278.historicalRoots: Spanish transhumant flock guardian, especially with Merino sheep.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 91: Spanish Mastiff
sources.evidence: FCI standard ties Merino transhumance and Mesta to wolf defense, and describes affection, confidence and determination when guarding.

VBO:0201315.summary: The Swedish Lapphund tends to be alert, affectionate and eager to engage with work; endurance and a ready response to training support its varied jobs. Sámi communities used it with reindeer, while northern households also valued it for hunting and watch duties. This range gave the breed a broader working history than herding alone.
VBO:0201315.historicalRoots: Sámi reindeer-herding, hunting and watch dog of Sweden.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 135: Swedish Lapphund
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents reindeer herding, hunting and watch roles, and characterizes the breed as alert, affectionate, willing, trainable and enduring.

VBO:0201342.summary: The Tenterfield Terrier tends to be quick, agile and alert, traits once put to work against vermin around Australian farms. Small ratting terriers arrived with English settlers and became a distinct local type; later dogs also took part in tracking and earthdog sports. Its inquisitive nature links the old pest-control job to those newer activities.
VBO:0201342.interestingFact: The name honors Tenterfield saddler George Woolnough, whose terriers were known in the district.
VBO:0201342.historicalRoots: Australian farm and homestead vermin-control terrier.

sources.title: National Tenterfield Terrier Council of Australia: Breed facts
sources.evidence: National Tenterfield Terrier Council describes settler-era ratters, quick agility and alertness, later tracking and earthdog sports.

sources.title: National Tenterfield Terrier Council: History
sources.evidence: Breed council history associates the Tenterfield name with local saddler George Woolnough and his terriers.

VBO:0201352.summary: The Tibetan Spaniel tends to be alert and loyal yet independent, sometimes aloof with strangers. Tibetan Spaniels served as both close companions and sentinels at Tibetan monasteries, watching from high walls and barking when something unusual approached. Its name is misleading: these were not European-style bird-flushing spaniels.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 231: Tibetan Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI describes Tibetan Spaniels as alert, loyal and independent companions, sometimes aloof with strangers.

sources.title: AKC: Tibetan Spaniel History
sources.evidence: AKC documents Tibetan monastery companionship, wall-top sentinel behavior and the breed’s misleading spaniel name.

VBO:0201361.summary: The Toy Fox Terrier tends to be quick and athletic, with an eagerness to learn that once brought some into circus performances. It grew from small Smooth Fox Terriers that proved useful as ratters on American farms. That mix of farm ratting, eager movement and trainable performance makes its history unusually varied.
VBO:0201361.historicalRoots: American small farm ratter developed from Smooth Fox Terrier stock.

sources.title: AKC Toy Fox Terrier official standard
sources.evidence: AKC Toy Fox Terrier standard supports its lively, quick and athletic disposition and Smooth Fox Terrier ancestry.

sources.title: AKC Toy Fox Terrier history
sources.evidence: AKC breed history documents farm ratting and later circus performance among Toy Fox Terriers.

VBO:0201390.summary: The Volpino Italiano tends to be lively and playful, closely attached to its people. It has long lived in both Italian noble houses and ordinary homes, serving as companion and alert little watchdog. Eighteenth-century carters in Tuscany and Latium valued the breed for announcing strangers along the road.
VBO:0201390.interestingFact: A Volpino appears in a Venetian painting by Vittore Carpaccio dated 1502.
VBO:0201390.historicalRoots: Italian household watchdog and companion with European spitz roots.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 195: Volpino Italiano
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents all-class Italian household use, watchdog/carrier history, family attachment, lively playfulness and Carpaccio painting.

VBO:0201412.summary: The Welsh Terrier tends to be game and fearless, with an affectionate, tractable side in close company. It once hunted fox, badger and even otter, requiring persistence with challenging quarry. Its old work called for a dog willing to press on underground and stay responsive to its handler.
VBO:0201412.historicalRoots: Welsh fox, badger and otter working terrier.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 78: Welsh Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies fox/badger/otter hunting and describes affectionate, controllable, game and fearless but nonaggressive temperament.

VBO:0201423.summary: The White Swiss Shepherd Dog tends to be balanced and friendly, attentive to its people and often quick to learn. Its modern role includes companionship and sport, with an eagerness for activity that carries into both. White shepherd lines were maintained in North America before Swiss breeders established the breed from the 1970s.
VBO:0201423.interestingFact: A North American male named Lobo, born in 1966, is cited as a progenitor of the Swiss population.
VBO:0201423.historicalRoots: North American white shepherd ancestry established as a Swiss breed.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 347: White Swiss Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents North American ancestry and Swiss establishment, companion/sporting role, trainability, activity, friendly balance and Lobo.

VBO:0201428.summary: The Wirehaired Vizsla tends to be affectionate and sensitive to rough handling, while retaining a keen hunting drive. It likes to stay in contact with its handler, search for game and hold a firm point. Hungarian breeders developed it in the 1930s for the older Vizsla’s versatile hunting role across rougher field conditions.
VBO:0201428.historicalRoots: Hungarian versatile pointing dog created in the 1930s.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 239: Wirehaired Vizsla
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents the 1930s founding cross, versatile gundog work, handler contact, passionate search, firm point, affection and dislike of rough treatment.

VBO:0201448.summary: The Yorkshire Terrier tends to be alert and spirited while keeping an even disposition. It emerged from nineteenth-century English terrier lines with an instinct for chasing rodents, later becoming a close companion. The quick attention to movement behind that original job remains part of its familiar terrier character.
VBO:0201448.historicalRoots: Yorkshire terrier developed in the mid-nineteenth century from several small terrier lines.

sources.title: FCI Standard No. 86: Yorkshire Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard traces Yorkshire ancestry, 1870 naming, rodent-hunting instinct and alert spirited even temperament.
